llm.reply:
The knowledge graph associates NCBIGene:7157, tumor protein p53, with Li-Fraumeni syndrome [4]. It also associates NCBIGene:11200, checkpoint kinase 2, with the syndrome [3]. A third associated gene is NCBIGene:1029, cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A [1].

## TP53 as primary cause

The literature describes Li-Fraumeni syndrome as a germline TP53 disorder [19: "cancer predisposition syndrome caused by a germline mutation of the TP53 gene on chromosome 17p13.1"]. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with high penetrance [19: "autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with high penetrance"]. Pathogenic TP53 variants abolish p53 function [19: "TP53 gene mutations cause the loss of function of p53"]. One case report identified a germline exon 5 missense variant [21: "germinal mutation c.527G>T (p.Cys176Phe) on exon 5 of the TP53 gene"].

## Phenotypic heterogeneity

Clinical expression varies even among carriers of the same TP53 variant [22: "Phenotypic heterogeneity is present among different families affected by the same pathogenic variant in TP53 gene"]. Proposed modifiers include TP53 and TP53-related gene polymorphisms, copy number changes and epigenetic dysregulation [22: "polymorphic variants in TP53 gene or in TP53-related genes, copy number variations in particular regions, and/or epigenetic deregulation of TP53 expression"].

## Clinical research

One trial is evaluating whole-body MRI surveillance in p53 mutation carriers [20: "Evaluation of Whole Body MRI for Early Detection of Cancers in Subjects With P53 Mutation"]. Another trial is examining the metabolic role of p53 in affected patients [11: "Role of p53 Gene in Metabolism Regulation in Patients With Li-Fraumeni Syndrome"].

The knowledge graph associates Li-Fraumeni syndrome with NCBIGene:7157, tumor protein p53 [4]. It also links NCBIGene:11200, checkpoint kinase 2 [3]. A third associated gene is NCBIGene:1029, cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A [1].

## Causal gene evidence

The literature identifies germline TP53 mutation as the cause [19: "caused by a germline mutation of the TP53 gene on chromosome 17p13.1"]. Inheritance is dominant and highly penetrant [19: "autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with high penetrance"]. A case report likewise attributes the condition to TP53 [21: "caused by germinal mutations in the TP53 gene"], describing what it calls a national first [21: "the first published case in Colombia of Li-Fraumeni syndrome with confirmed molecular diagnosis"].

## Phenotypic heterogeneity

Clinical presentation varies even with a shared variant [22: "Phenotypic heterogeneity is present among different families affected by the same pathogenic variant in TP53 gene"]. Proposed modifiers include other genetic factors [22: "polymorphic variants in TP53 gene or in TP53-related genes, copy number variations in particular regions"].
